title: Carrying the Weight: A Part-Time Hospital Porter and Carer Living with Long COVID
transcript:
[00:00:05] INT: Right, so the recorder is running now. Thank you again for taking the time to speak with me today, Graham. Just to confirm for the recording, you've read the information sheet from the University of Callowhill and you're happy to go ahead?
[00:00:18] P: Yes, yeah, that's fine, Claire. I'm Graham Whitaker, sixty-two, and yeah, happy to do it. If it helps somebody else down the line, then it's worth an hour of my time, isn't it?
[00:00:31] INT: Absolutely. And if you need a break at any point, just say the word. To start us off, could you tell me a bit about your job and what life looked like before you got ill?
[00:00:44] P: Sure. Well, I've been a hospital porter at Northbridge General Hospital for, oh, coming up to nineteen years now. Westmere Valley NHS Trust, that's who employs us. Specifically I'm on Acute Logistics and Portering Team B. Before all this, I was full-time, thirty-seven and a half hours, doing the early shifts mostly—six till two—moving patients to theatre, taking bloods down to pathology, lugging oxygen cylinders, all that. I loved it, honestly. I'm not a sit-at-a-desk sort of bloke. I liked being on my feet, having a bit of banter with the nurses, feeling like I was actually doing something useful. Even had my own little niche—I'm the only porter on the early handover who knows how to properly clear and reset the old pneumatic tube canister system when it jams on the third floor, because the estates lads showed me years ago. You know, you feel like part of the furniture in a good way.
[00:01:48] INT: And outside of work?
[00:01:51] P: Well, my wife Brenda, she's got rheumatoid arthritis, quite bad in her hands and knees, so I've been her main carer for the last five or six years. Before I got ill, it was manageable, you know? I'd finish my shift at two, come back to our place on 14 Birchwood Close—we're just over in Millbrook, bit of a quiet estate in Westmere—and I'd do the shopping, cook the tea, help her with the bath if she was having a flare-up. And in the evenings, if I had a spare hour, I've got a little shed out back where I do my hobby. I'm into restoring vintage 1950s brass maritime barometers. Bit niche, I know! My dad was in the Merchant Navy, so I grew up around them. I'm even the treasurer for the Westmere Horological and Barometer Society, though I haven't been to a meeting since last autumn. Just haven't had the puff for it.
[00:02:50] INT: When did you first catch COVID, and how did things change from there?
[00:02:56] P: I remember the exact day because it was my daughter Chloe's birthday—she lives over in Kelmscott now, bless her. It was the 14th of November 2021. We'd had a little lunch, and that evening I just felt like I'd been hit by a bus. Tested positive the next morning. I didn't end up in hospital, thankfully, because who would've looked after Brenda? Chloe had to drive over and leave shopping on the doorstep. I thought, right, two weeks, I'll shake it off. I've always been fit as a butcher's dog. Never took a sick day in ten years. Except... I didn't shake it off. Come January, I was still getting this crushing breathlessness just walking up the stairs to our bedroom. And the fatigue—it's not normal tiredness, Claire. It's like somebody's pulled the plug out of the wall and poured concrete into your boots.
[00:03:54] INT: That sounds really frightening, especially when you've always been so active. What happened when you tried to go back to work?
[00:04:02] P: Well, I went back on the 3rd of March 2022, probably too soon, if I'm honest. I was worried about going onto half pay. I thought I could just push through it—that's what you do, isn't it? You get your head down and graft. My manager, Sharon Patel, she's alright, Sharon, she's got a lot on her plate managing the whole portering rota, so I didn't want to make a fuss. I didn't even tell her how bad it was at first. I just said I was a bit chesty. First week back, I was pushing a bariatric bed up the ramp to Ward Four with my mate Tariq Mahmood, and I literally had to let go and lean against the wall. My heart was hammering—proper tachycardia, they called it later—and I couldn't catch my breath. Tariq covered for me, bless him, said to the sister that I'd tweaked my knee. I was mortified. Sixty years old and I couldn't push a bed.
[00:05:05] INT: Did you end up disclosing what was going on to Sharon after that?
[00:05:10] P: I had to, yeah. Because the next day I couldn't get out of bed. That's what the clinic later told me is post-exertional malaise. You do too much on Tuesday, and by Wednesday afternoon you're flat on your back with flu-like aches and this horrible brain fog. I couldn't remember the door codes to the pharmacy. I've used those codes every day for fifteen years and I was standing there staring at the keypad like an idiot. So I went to Sharon's office and just broke down, honestly. Never cried in front of a boss in my life. I told her I'd been diagnosed with Long COVID by my GP, Dr. Hannah Okafor, over at Oakfield Medical Practice. Sharon was decent about it, to be fair. She referred me to Occupational Health.
[00:06:02] INT: How was that process with Occupational Health?
[00:06:06] P: Slow. Very slow. I've still got the paperwork right here actually—I brought my folder in case you needed dates. Yeah, my Occupational Health reference was OH-2022-8841. They didn't actually do a full review with me until the 18th of September 2023, which was ages after the initial referral, though we had a couple of quick phone calls before that. The nurse was nice enough, suggested phased return, lighter duties—like doing the post run or sitting on the main reception desk directing visitors. Problem is, on Acute Logistics and Portering Team B, there aren't many light duties! If I'm not pushing beds, somebody else like Tariq has to pick up the slack. And you feel the resentment, even if nobody says it to your face. Well, one of the younger lads did make a comment in the breakroom about 'part-time skivers', and it really got to me.
[00:07:08] INT: Oh, that's awful. Did you end up reducing your hours formally?
[00:07:13] P: Yeah, on the 1st of April 2024 I dropped down to twenty hours a week. Four hours a day, Monday to Friday, just doing the morning blood runs and the pharmacy deliveries with the little electric tug, so I'm not doing the heavy lifting. It's the only way I can keep my head above water and still have anything left in the tank for Brenda when I get home. Because if I crash at work, Brenda doesn't get her dinner. Simple as that.
[00:07:43] INT: Can you tell me a bit about the financial impact of dropping to twenty hours?
[00:07:49] P: It's been brutal, Claire, I won't lie to you. I'm on Band 2, which works out to about £11.45 an hour. When I was full-time with the unsocial hours enhancements, we were alright. Now, my take-home pay is roughly £1,120 a month, give or take. I do claim Carer's Allowance for Brenda, which is £81.90 a week, and thank goodness for that, because otherwise we'd be in serious trouble. You've got to be careful though—if I do even one extra shift of overtime to help out, I go over the earnings limit for Carer's Allowance and they claw it all back. It's a trap, really. Our gas and electric alone went up to £240 a month last winter because Brenda can't be in a cold house with her joints. We've had to dip into the little bit of savings we had put by for retirement. I'm sixty-two, I should be winding down, not worrying about whether we can afford the car MOT.
[00:08:56] INT: That's a huge amount of pressure to carry alongside managing your own health. What kind of medical support have you had for the Long COVID?
[00:09:05] P: Mixed, to be honest. Dr. Hannah Okafor at Oakfield Medical Practice has been brilliant—she actually believed me from day one, which I know a lot of people don't get. She put me on a low dose of Amitriptyline at night to help with the nerve pain and the sleep, and gave me a Salbutamol inhaler for when my chest gets tight. She also referred me to St. Jude's Post-COVID Assessment Clinic. Took nine months on the waiting list to get seen, mind you. When I finally got there, they ran all the heart and lung scans—I remember having to read out my NHS number, 999 482 1903, about twenty times that week—and everything came back 'normal'. Which is great, you don't want heart failure, obviously, but it's also frustrating because you're sitting there with chronic fatigue and brain fog and they basically hand you a leaflet on pacing and discharge you back to your GP.
[00:10:09] INT: And how has all of this affected your relationship with Brenda, and how you see yourself?
[00:10:17] P: That's the hardest bit, really. [sighs] I've always been the strong one. The fixer. If the boiler broke, I'd look at it. If Brenda couldn't open a jar or get her coat on, I was right there. Now, there are days when I'm lying on the sofa at three in the afternoon, eyes closed, and Brenda's in the kitchen trying to make us both a cup of tea with her swollen hands, and it just breaks my heart. I feel like I'm failing her. She never complains, she tells me not to be daft, that we're a team. Chloe's been great too, she comes up from Kelmscott every other Sunday to batch-cook some stews for the freezer. But it changes you, doesn't it? I look in the mirror and I don't recognise the bloke looking back. I used to spend hours in my shed working on a delicate barometer mechanism with tiny brass screws. Now my hands shake if I'm tired, and I lose track of what I'm doing halfway through. I've got a 1954 Kelvin Hughes barometer sitting on the workbench that's been in pieces for over a year. Just haven't got the brainpower to put it back together.
[00:11:32] INT: It sounds like it's touched every single corner of your life—work, home, your hobbies, your sense of who you are. Looking ahead, what do you think you need from your employer or the NHS to keep going?
[00:11:46] P: Flexibility, mostly. And a bit of understanding that Long COVID isn't just a bad cold you get over in a month. Sharon's been good with the twenty hours, and I'm grateful I've still got a job at Northbridge General Hospital, because I need the structure and I need the money. I just wish there was proper sick pay protection for people like us, so you're not terrified of triggering an absence review every time you have a flare-up. Oh, and by the way, Claire, if you need to send me that summary of the study findings later on, my email is g.whitaker62@example.com, or you can text me on 07700 900418—I'm better with texts than phone calls these days, gives me time to think before I reply.
[00:12:34] INT: I've got both of those noted down, Graham, thank you. Is there anything else you'd like to add before I switch the recorder off?
[00:12:41] P: No, I think I've talked your ear off enough! Just... I hope somebody listens to us. There's a lot of NHS staff out there quietly struggling, trying to look after patients and their own families while running on empty. Thank you for letting me get it off my chest.
[00:12:58] INT: Thank you so much, Graham. I'll stop the recording now.

identifiers.text: Acute Logistics and Portering Team B
